items.passage: Economists Michela Giorcelli and Petra Moser found that after Lombardy and Venetia adopted copyright law in 1801 under French rule, the two states’ output of new operas rose far faster than that of other Italian states. Since later extensions of copyright terms brought no comparable gains, basic protection, not its prolongation, appears to have been ______ creativity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A spur to something is an incentive that drives it on. Copyright arrived in Lombardy and Venetia under French rule, and afterward the two states’ production of new operas rose far faster than elsewhere in Italy, so the protection encouraged composers’ work. Because later extensions brought no further gains, the text credits basic protection, not longer terms, with that effect.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that copyright took the place of creative work; the law and a rise in new operas went together.

B.why_wrong: A constraint on creativity would hold it back, but opera output rose faster after the law was adopted, not more slowly.

D.why_wrong: A symptom of creativity would be a result of it. The law came with French rule, and the rise in new operas followed it, so the protection preceded the creativity rather than reflecting it.

sources.what: NBER Digest (May 2020) on Giorcelli and Moser: Lombardy and Venetia adopted copyright in 1801 after coming under French rule; new operas rose sharply there relative to other Italian states; more durable and popular operas; no comparable benefit from longer copyright terms

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the rise follows the law, and the law came from conquest, so protection drove output; then reject the reverse direction). Corrected ranks: substitute 9,221; constraint 9,447; spur 6,779; symptom 16,017. Band 6 (plain phrase keys, reasoning carries the item). Detail simplified: output figures (threefold against about 50 percent) given as 'far faster'.

band7.why: Raw ranks a spur to 6,779; a substitute for 9,221; a constraint on 9,447; a symptom of 16,017: 1 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 3.99 (the band-6 mean). Plain phrase key with the reasoning carrying it, as the band-6 B6 items do: the student maps basic protection to the 1801 law and rejects the reversed direction (a symptom of). Constraint falls to one stated fact. A band 6 as targeted, on the weaker side.

items.passage: Studying professional basketball and soccer teams, organizational behavior researcher Roderick Swaab and colleagues found the link between a team’s share of top players and its success to be ______: adding stars helped only up to a point, after which coordination suffered and results declined. In baseball, where players depend less on one another, additional talent never hurt.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A nonlinear relationship is one that does not change at a steady rate in one direction. The text says that more top players improved results only up to a point and then made them worse, so success first rose and then fell as talent increased.

B.why_wrong: An inverse link would mean more talent always brought less success. In basketball and soccer, success rose with talent at first and fell only past a certain point.

C.why_wrong: A spurious link is one that only appears to exist. The text reports a real pattern in which talent first helped and then hurt; nothing suggests the connection was illusory.

D.why_wrong: A proportional link, in which success rises steadily with talent, is closer to the baseball pattern, where extra talent never hurt. In basketball and soccer, results declined once teams had too many stars.

sources.what: APS press release on Swaab, Schaerer, Anicich, Ronay and Galinsky (2014), Psychological Science: top talent helps team performance only up to a point in basketball and soccer, then hurts as coordination suffers; not in baseball

items.notes: Subject: social science (organizational psychology). Key letter A. Restatement after the colon, read as a shape (rise then fall). Two distractors each fit half the pattern (inverse, the decline; proportional, the rise and baseball). Raw ranks: nonlinear 72,820; inverse 49,909; spurious 20,718; proportional 68,085 (corrected about 15,600; 20,900; 20,700; 17,800). Band 6.

band7.why: Raw ranks nonlinear 72,820; inverse 49,909; spurious 20,718; proportional 68,085 (corrected about 15,600 to 20,900): check 1 passes, but three of the four are school mathematics words a 1400 scorer knows, so the rarity is a corpus artifact (check 6 finds at most one unknown word). One-step colon restatement read as a shape, two half-right distractors. Band 6 as targeted.

fixes: notes: the ranks labelled corrected were raw; relabelled and added corrected values
distractor D why_wrong no longer says the text calls baseball proportional (it says only that extra talent never hurt)

items.passage: Asgard archaea, identified in 2015 from DNA dredged up near an Arctic Ocean hydrothermal vent, carry many genes otherwise associated with complex cells, and some biologists consider them the closest living relatives of those cells’ ancestors. Until Hiroyuki Imachi and colleagues grew one in the laboratory after twelve years of effort, however, any picture of the organisms themselves was ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Conjectural means based on inference rather than direct evidence. Before Imachi’s team grew one of these microbes, Asgard archaea were known only from DNA, so any idea of what the organisms themselves were like had to be inferred from their genes rather than observed.

A.recipe: near miss: false rather than unproven (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: Fallacious means mistaken. The text says the organisms had not been grown and observed, not that earlier ideas about them turned out to be wrong.

B.why_wrong: Incontrovertible means beyond dispute. Knowledge drawn only from DNA, before anyone had grown the organism, is the opposite of settled.

C.why_wrong: Perfunctory means done with little care or interest. Nothing suggests that biologists were careless; the limit was that the organisms had never been grown.

band7_moves: option set all past rank 14,000 (rare words throughout)
blank on the earlier, superseded state, with the finding given only as the turning point (until ... however)
implicit clue: knowledge from DNA alone implies an inferred picture, never stated
near-synonym distractor failing on one feature (fallacious: false, not unproven)

sources.what: Science News on Imachi et al. (2020, Nature): Asgard archaea found in 2015 from genetic material from an Arctic Ocean hydrothermal vent; many eukaryotic genes; argued to be closest living relatives of the archaea that gave rise to complex life; about 12 years of lab work to grow one

items.notes: Subject: natural science (microbiology). Key letter D. Contrast frame (however) with the blank on the earlier state of knowledge; the clue is implicit: DNA alone means any picture of the cell was inferred. Corrected ranks: fallacious 42,005; incontrovertible 36,669; perfunctory 14,278; conjectural 41,050: all four past 10,000, mean log about 4.5. Band-5 guard: clear (key not the lone rare option). Near miss: fallacious (false rather than unverified).

band7.why: Raw ranks fallacious 42,005; incontrovertible 36,669; perfunctory 14,278; conjectural 41,050: 4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000, mean log 4.49; band-5 guard clear. B3 shape of 6c9f1727 (Until ... the thing was notional): blank on the earlier state of knowledge, the clue implicit (known only from DNA, the organisms themselves not yet grown). Fallacious is the near miss that fails on one feature (false, not unproven), incontrovertible the reversal, perfunctory a rare unsupported word.

items.passage: Kernza, a perennial grain that The Land Institute developed from intermediate wheatgrass, need not be replanted each year, and its deep, dense roots help build healthy soil, but it is unlikely to ______ annual wheat anytime soon: even under ideal conditions, it yields only about 30 percent as much grain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To supplant something is to take its place. Kernza has real advantages, but it produces only about 30 percent as much grain as wheat even under ideal conditions, so it is unlikely to replace annual wheat as a crop in the near future.

A.why_wrong: To complement wheat is to add to it alongside it. A lower yield is a reason Kernza cannot replace wheat, not a reason it could not be grown in addition to wheat.

C.why_wrong: Whether Kernza looks like or resembles wheat is not discussed, and its lower grain yield has nothing to do with resemblance.

D.why_wrong: Kernza is perennial and does not need replanting each year, so it already outlasts annual wheat; saying it is unlikely to outlast wheat contradicts the text.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Kernza: intermediate wheatgrass grain developed by The Land Institute; perennial; deeper and more abundant roots support healthy soil; as much as 30 percent of the yield of traditional wheat under ideal conditions

items.notes: Subject: natural science (agriculture). Key letter B. Negated frame stated plainly (unlikely to), as in 3.21; the colon gives the reason, which the student must connect to replacement rather than to coexistence. Raw ranks: complement 19,388; supplant 28,305; resemble 11,654; outlast 39,183 (corrected complement about 9,400, resemble about 10,100). Band 6.

band7.why: Raw ranks complement 19,388; supplant 28,305; resemble 11,654; outlast 39,183 (corrected complement about 9,400, resemble about 10,100): 3 of 4 past 10,000, but resemble, outlast and complement are familiar words. Plain negated frame (unlikely to) with the reason after the colon, the band-6 B5 pattern of bbb77c84 (superseded). Band 6 as targeted.

fixes: notes: the ranks labelled corrected were raw; relabelled and added corrected values for complement and resemble

items.passage:
The following text is from Ford Madox Ford’s 1915 novel The Good Soldier. The narrator, an American, recalls the years that he and his wife spent in the company of an English couple, the Ashburnhams.

So began those nine years of uninterrupted tranquillity. They were characterized by an extraordinary <u>want</u> of any communicativeness on the part of the Ashburnhams to which we, on our part, replied by leaving out quite as extraordinarily, and nearly as completely, the personal note. Indeed, you may take it that what characterized our relationship was an atmosphere of taking everything for granted.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “want” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “want” means lack. The narrator says that he and his wife answered the Ashburnhams by “leaving out quite as extraordinarily” the personal note, so the Ashburnhams too must have held back from sharing anything personal. The friendship was marked by a deficiency of communicativeness, not by any desire for it.

B.why_wrong: “Want” can mean a strong desire, but the narrator describes the Ashburnhams as uncommunicative, a quality he and his wife matched by leaving out the personal note; nothing suggests the Ashburnhams longed to communicate.

C.why_wrong: “Want” can mean poverty, but the sentence concerns how little the Ashburnhams shared about themselves, not a lack of money.

D.why_wrong: “Want” can mean a pressing need, but the text does not say communication was urgently required; it says it was almost entirely missing.

band7_moves: familiar word in an older secondary sense (want as lack), everyday sense offered as a distractor
clue a clause away, in the narrator’s ironic matching of the couple’s reserve
every distractor a real sense of the target (desire, poverty, need)
option set all past rank 20,000; key a mid-frequency word, not a plain synonym

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #2775, Ford Madox Ford, The Good Soldier (1915), part I, chapter IV; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter A. Older secondary sense of a common word (want as lack) against its everyday sense (desire); the clue is the narrator’s parallel clause (replied by leaving out ... the personal note). All three distractors are real senses of “want” (desire, poverty, need). Corrected ranks: deficiency 23,080; hankering 21,045; indigence 63,234; exigency 32,335: all four past 20,000. Literary work not used in any official item (no Ford in material/rw).

band7.why: Raw ranks Deficiency 23,080; Hankering 21,045; Indigence 63,234; Exigency 32,335: 4 of 4 past 20,000, mean log 4.50, rarer than both CB band-7 M1 models (6557f7fc, 7f935017). Common target in its older sense (want as lack) against the everyday sense (Hankering), and two need senses (Indigence: poverty; Exigency: pressing need) that fail on one feature each. The clue is the parallel clause (we replied by leaving out the personal note). The "want of any" frame helps a reader who knows "for want of", the one thing keeping it from the top of band 7.

review.excerpt_checked: exact against Project Gutenberg 2775, part I, chapter IV; author, title and year correct

items.passage: Colombian artist Oscar Muñoz’s installation Aliento (1995–2002) consists of small oval mirrors that appear entirely conventional until viewers lean in and exhale onto them. At that moment the mirrors no longer ______ the individuals peering into them: as condensation clouds each surface, the viewer’s own image disappears, replaced by a photographic portrait of someone who has died.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To reflect a person is to show that person’s image, as a mirror normally does. Once a viewer exhales onto one of Muñoz’s mirrors, the viewer’s own image disappears and a portrait of someone else appears, so the mirror stops showing the person looking into it.

A.why_wrong: Breathing on the mirror makes the viewer’s image disappear, so the mirrors do obscure the viewers at that moment; saying they no longer obscure them contradicts the text.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the mirrors ever made viewers look better than they are; the change described is that the viewer’s image disappears entirely.

C.why_wrong: The text says viewers lean in and exhale onto the mirrors; it says nothing about the mirrors ceasing to fascinate the people who look into them.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Oscar Muñoz (artist): Aliento (Breath), 1995–2002, small oval mirrors screen printed with grease; when a viewer breathes on one, the viewer’s reflection is erased and a portrait of a dead person, taken from newspaper obituaries, appears

items.notes: Subject: humanities (visual art). Key letter D. Negated frame (no longer), with the clue after the colon; the key is the everyday function of a mirror, which the student must see the work suspend. Corrected ranks: obscure 5,213; flatter 8,339; captivate 31,527; reflect 5,527. Detail simplified: the portraits are of people who died in Colombia’s political violence (not stated).

items.passage: Shilai Zhang and colleagues determined that from a single planting, the perennial rice variety PR23 produced grain for eight consecutive harvests over four years, averaging 6.8 metric tons per hectare per harvest. These results made its productivity ______ that of conventional annual rice, which averaged 6.7 metric tons but required replanting for every crop.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be on a par with something is to be about equal to it. PR23 averaged 6.8 metric tons per hectare per harvest and conventional annual rice averaged 6.7, so the perennial rice was about as productive as the annual rice it was compared with.

A.why_wrong: PR23 was bred from other rice, but the sentence compares the size of two yields; one variety’s productivity is not produced from another’s.

C.why_wrong: A fraction of annual rice’s productivity would be much smaller, but 6.8 metric tons is about the same as 6.7.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that PR23’s productivity depended on how much annual rice produced; the two were simply measured and compared.

sources.what: Zhang et al., Sustained productivity and agronomic potential of perennial rice, Nature Sustainability (published online November 2022): from a single planting, perennial rice produced grain for eight consecutive harvests over four years, averaging 6.8 Mg per hectare per harvest versus 6.7 Mg for replanted annual rice

items.notes: Subject: natural science (agriculture). Key letter B. Restatement by numbers: the student compares 6.8 with 6.7. Corrected ranks: derived 2,000 or so (derive); par 12,383; fraction 12,184; contingent 17,762. Mixed phrase frames, as in 2.20.

items.passage: Canadian artist Brian Jungen’s Prototypes for New Understanding (1998–2005) are masks hand-stitched from disassembled Nike Air Jordan sneakers and shaped to recall the mask designs of coastal nations of British Columbia. Jungen exhibited them on metal armatures inside transparent display cases, much as anthropology museums have traditionally displayed Indigenous artifacts, making their presentation ______ that museum convention.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: An allusion to something is an indirect reference to it. The text says Jungen showed his sneaker masks on metal armatures (supporting frames) inside transparent display cases, “much as” anthropology museums have traditionally displayed Indigenous artifacts, so his presentation deliberately called that museum convention to mind.

A.why_wrong: A departure would be a break from museum practice, but Jungen used the same method museums use: objects on metal supports inside clear display cases.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Jungen’s presentation got in the way of the museum convention; it borrows that convention.

D.why_wrong: A precursor comes before what it leads to, but the museum convention is described as traditional; Jungen’s works came later, from 1998 to 2005.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Brian Jungen: Prototypes for New Understanding (1998–2005), masks made from Nike Air Jordan sneakers, evocative of mask designs of coastal nations of British Columbia; early works shown as if anthropological artifacts, on metal armatures inside Plexiglas vitrines

items.notes: Subject: humanities (visual art). Key letter C. The similarity is stated (much as); the student must choose the word for a deliberate reference to that convention. Revised after a blind solve: the earlier version left the museum display practice to outside knowledge. Corrected ranks: departure 1,837; obstacle 8,054; allusion 6,623; precursor 38,574.

fixes: register: in configurations that recall to and shaped to recall, Plexiglas vitrines to transparent display cases; the passage was the densest in the medium tier (6.27 chars per word, now 6.12), and the tier moves from 5.41 to 5.35 chars per word against CB 5.30 while keeping CB long-word share
explanation updated to the new wording

items.passage: In 1964 landscape architect Cornelia Hahn Oberlander persuaded Vancouver’s municipal government to ______ the driftwood logs that had washed up on its beaches. Rather than burning the logs, the city kept them at her insistence and put them to use as seating and shelter for visitors to its shoreline.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To repurpose something is to give it a new use. Instead of being burned, the driftwood logs were kept and put to use as seating and shelter for visitors, a use quite different from their former place as debris.

B.why_wrong: To incinerate is to burn, which is exactly what the city did not do; the logs were kept rather than burned.

C.why_wrong: To restore something is to return it to an earlier condition. The logs were not repaired or returned to any former state; they were put to a new use.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the logs were sold; the city kept them on its beaches for public use.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Cornelia Oberlander: in 1964 she persuaded Vancouver to keep driftwood logs for seating and shelter instead of burning them

items.notes: Subject: humanities (landscape architecture). Key letter A. Restatement in the next sentence (kept rather than burned, used as seats and shelter). Corrected ranks: repurpose unseen (modern); incinerate unseen; restore about 5,000; auction 11,781.

fixes: precision: the clue now says the city put the logs to use as seating and shelter (source: kept them and reused them as benches and shelters); before, the logs only "over time came to serve", which made repurpose the best word by elimination rather than a precise fit

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sarah Grand’s 1897 novel The Beth Book. Beth, who is twelve, has gone to stay with her great-aunt Victoria.

Aunt Victoria was surprised herself to find how kindly Beth <u>took to</u> a regular life, how exact she was in the performance of her little housekeeping duties, and how punctual in everything; she had never suspected that Beth’s whole leaning was towards law and order.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “took to” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Aunt Victoria is surprised by “how kindly” Beth took to a regular life: Beth turns out to be exact in her housekeeping duties and punctual in everything, because her “whole leaning” is toward law and order. So Beth readily adapted to an orderly routine.

A.why_wrong: “Took to” can mean fled into, as in taking to the woods, but Beth is not escaping anything; she is settling comfortably into an orderly routine.

B.why_wrong: “Took to” can mean carried someone to a place, but nothing is being carried here; the phrase describes Beth’s response to a way of living.

C.why_wrong: “Took to” can mean turned to out of need, but Beth is not driven to a regular life by desperation; she takes to it “kindly,” because it suits her leaning toward order.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #28088, Sarah Grand, The Beth Book (1897), chapter XXII; excerpt copied exactly except that the sentence is ended after “law and order”; Beth is twelve and travels with Great-Aunt Victoria Bench in chapter XXI

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter D. Phrasal target with four senses as options, as in 2.8 and 2.26. Adapted: the source sentence continues after “law and order” with “nor observed that...”; it is ended there.

review.excerpt_checked: exact against Project Gutenberg 28088, chapter XXII (sentence ended at "law and order", marked adapted); author, title and year correct

items.passage: In the summer of 2011, a Sargassum seaweed bloom large enough to be detected in satellite imagery appeared in the tropical Atlantic Ocean for the first time. Since then, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt has become ______: composed of numerous floating patches, some covering an acre, it was estimated to weigh 24.2 million tons in June 2022.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Enormous means extremely large. After the colon, the text says the belt is composed of numerous patches, some covering an acre, and that it was estimated to weigh 24.2 million tons, which shows how huge it has become.

A.why_wrong: Scarce means hard to find. A belt of seaweed weighing 24.2 million tons is the opposite of scarce.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the seaweed being easily damaged; it describes the belt’s size.

D.why_wrong: The text does not discuss whether the belt’s appearance or size can be predicted; the information after the colon is about how large it is.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt: in summer 2011 a bloom large enough to be noticeable in satellite imagery appeared for the first time; many patches, some up to an acre; in June 2022 the belt was estimated to weigh 24.2 million tons

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oceanography). Key letter B. Restatement after the colon (patches up to an acre, 24.2 million tons). Corrected ranks: scarce about 5,000; enormous about 2,500; fragile 9,404; predictable unseen (modern, easy).

items.passage: Physician Rebecca Lee Crumpler wrote A Book of Medical Discourses (1883) for mothers and nurses rather than for fellow physicians, and the book places particular emphasis on ______. Crumpler encouraged readers to understand the structure of the human body, arguing that many ailments have identifiable causes that can be eliminated before the ailments ever develop.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Prevention means stopping something before it happens. Crumpler wanted readers to understand the body so that the causes of many ailments could be eliminated before the ailments developed, so her book emphasizes preventing illness.

A.why_wrong: Surgery belongs to medicine, but the book was written for mothers and nurses, and the text describes keeping illness from starting, not operating on patients.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text describes the book as focused on scientific research; it gives readers practical knowledge of the body.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say Crumpler stressed following orders; she urged readers to understand the body for themselves.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Rebecca Lee Crumpler: A Book of Medical Discourses (1883) written for nurses and mothers; emphasized the possibilities of prevention; urged women to understand the structure of the body; every ailment has a cause that can often be removed

items.notes: Subject: history (medicine). Key letter C. Restatement in the next sentence (causes removed before ailments develop). The item hangs on the book, not on Crumpler’s firsts. Corrected ranks: surgery 19,358; research 2,475; prevention 32,906; obedience 4,121.

items.passage: Toshio Mori’s short story collection Yokohama, California, which portrays the everyday experiences of Japanese Americans, was scheduled for publication before World War II, but the war ______ its release: the collection did not appear until 1949, accompanied by an introduction from the celebrated writer William Saroyan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Delayed means made later than planned. The collection was supposed to come out before World War II but did not appear until 1949, so the war pushed its release back.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the war paid for the book; the text says only that the book came out years later than planned.

B.why_wrong: The text does not say the war gave Mori the idea for the stories, and the blank concerns the book’s release, which came years late.

C.why_wrong: Accelerated means sped up, but the release was scheduled before the war and did not happen until 1949.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Toshio Mori: Yokohama, California had a tentative publication date, but World War II halted publication; published in 1949 by Caxton Printers with an introduction by William Saroyan; his stories portray everyday lives of Japanese Americans

items.notes: Subject: humanities (literature, publishing history). Key letter D. Restatement in the next sentence (did not appear until 1949). Corrected ranks: funded 7,219; inspired 3,563; accelerated 30,748; delayed 2,128.

items.passage: In a 2005 experiment, cognitive scientists Petter Johansson and Lars Hall asked participants to identify the more attractive of two faces, then secretly handed them the photograph they had rejected. Most participants failed to notice the substitution. Instead, they readily ______ the choice they had never made, explaining, for instance, that they preferred blondes when they had actually selected a dark-haired woman.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To defend a choice is to give reasons for it. After the switch, participants explained why they had supposedly picked the face in front of them, offering reasons such as a preference for blondes, so they defended a choice they had not actually made.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the participants were sorry about their choice; they explained it as though it were their real preference.

C.why_wrong: The participants did not change the choice; they accepted the switched photograph and gave reasons for picking it.

D.why_wrong: The participants did not forget the choice; they talked about it and explained it.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Choice blindness: Johansson, Hall, Sikström and Olsson (2005) had participants choose the more attractive of two face photographs, then swapped in the other photo by sleight of hand; a majority failed to notice and explained the choice they had not made, e.g. preferring blondes after pointing to a dark-haired woman

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology). Key letter A. Restatement after the comma (explaining ... that they preferred blondes). Corrected ranks: defended 9,450; regretted 5,666; reversed 7,086; forgot 1,437.

items.passage:
The following text is from Sinclair Lewis’s 1919 novel Free Air. Claire Boltwood is driving west with her father, Mr. Boltwood, and has just reached Fargo, North Dakota, proud of how far she has come.

Mr. Boltwood <u>caught</u> her enthusiasm. Dinner was a festival, and in iced tea the peaceful conquistadores drank the toast of the new Spanish Main; and afterward, arm in arm, went chattering to the movies.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “caught” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Claire is proud and excited about the trip, and the text then shows father and daughter celebrating together: dinner is “a festival,” they drink a toast, and they go “arm in arm, … chattering” to the movies. Mr. Boltwood came to share her enthusiasm.

A.why_wrong: One can catch a ball by grabbing it, but enthusiasm is a feeling, not an object Mr. Boltwood takes hold of with his hands.

B.why_wrong: One can catch a train or bus by boarding it, but here the object of “caught” is Claire’s enthusiasm, not a vehicle.

D.why_wrong: One can catch an animal by trapping it, but Mr. Boltwood does not capture Claire’s feeling; he begins to feel it too.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #26732, Sinclair Lewis, Free Air (1919), chapter VI; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. All three distractors are other senses of “caught” (grab, board, trap). Context line paraphrases the preceding paragraph (Claire crossing into North Dakota, finding a good hotel in Fargo and feeling she has earned it).

review.excerpt_checked: exact against Project Gutenberg 26732; author, title and year correct

items.passage:
The following text is from Ouida’s 1900 novel The Waters of Edera. Adone, a young Italian farmer, has heard from a girl named Nerina that strangers were measuring the riverbank on his land.

He went to the spot where the intruders had been seen, but there was no trace of them, except that the wet sand <u>bore</u> footprints of persons who had, as she had said of them, worn boots.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “bore” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Adone finds no trace of the strangers except the marks they left: the wet sand had their footprints in it. In this context, “bore” means showed or carried visibly on its surface.

A.why_wrong: A person can bear, or endure, hardship, but the sand is not suffering anything; it simply has footprints on it.

C.why_wrong: “Bore” can mean gave birth to or produced, as in bearing a child, but the sand did not produce the footprints; the strangers left them.

D.why_wrong: A beam can bear, or support, a weight, but the text describes marks visible in the sand, not sand holding something up.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #13459, Ouida, The Waters of Edera (1900), chapter III; excerpt copied exactly; Nerina reports strangers who seemed to measure the banks

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter B. Concrete sense of a common verb, as in 1.4 and 1.38; all three distractors are other senses of “bear.”

review.excerpt_checked: exact against Project Gutenberg 13459; author, title and year correct

items.passage:
The following text is from Charles Egbert Craddock’s 1885 novel Down the Ravine. Each spring a poor widow in the Tennessee mountains hires a mule from a neighboring tanner who needs the animal himself, and she pays with her son Birt’s labor.

Nevertheless, this bargain was annually <u>struck</u>. The poverty-stricken widow always congratulated herself upon its conclusion, and it never occurred to her that the amount of work that Birt did in the tanyard was a disproportionately large return for the few days that the tanner’s mule ploughed their little fields.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “struck” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: A bargain that is struck is one that the two sides reach, or agree to. The widow congratulates herself every year on “its conclusion,” so each spring she and the tanner came to the same agreement.

A.why_wrong: “Struck” can mean hit, as with a fist or a hammer, but a bargain is an agreement, not something that can be hit.

B.why_wrong: Something can be struck from a list, or erased, but the text says the widow congratulated herself on the bargain each year, so it was made, not removed.

C.why_wrong: Miners strike gold when they find it, but the bargain was not found; the widow and the tanner made it with each other every spring.

items.passage: In 1966 Marie Van Brittan Brown and her husband, Albert, filed a patent for a home security system. In their design, a camera viewed visitors through peepholes in the front door and transmitted their image to a television monitor inside. Brown, whose irregular work hours sometimes left her home alone in Queens, New York, wanted to feel less ______ unfamiliar visitors.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be vulnerable to someone is to be exposed to possible harm from that person. Brown was sometimes home alone, and her system let her see who was at the door without opening it, so it was meant to make her less exposed to danger from strangers.

B.why_wrong: The system let Brown see visitors, but the text presents it as a security device, not a way to satisfy curiosity about who visited.

C.why_wrong: A camera and monitor would not make Brown know the visitors better; it let her see them before deciding whether to open the door.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Brown wanted to feel less thankful for visitors; the text describes her concern about being home alone.

Brown; camera moving between peepholes, images sent to a television monitor so the occupant could see who was at the door without opening it; she worked irregular hours and was sometimes home alone in Jamaica, Queens

items.passage: Woodworker George Nakashima constructed many of his tables from wide slabs of timber whose natural, irregular edges he left unfinished, and he frequently selected boards marked by knots and swirling grain. His furniture thus reflects a deep ______ the individual character of each piece of wood.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Nakashima kept the natural edges of his slabs and chose boards with knots and swirling grain instead of hiding those features. His furniture therefore shows respect for the distinctive qualities of each piece of wood.

A.why_wrong: Indifference would mean not caring about the wood’s character, but Nakashima deliberately kept natural edges and chose boards for their knots and grain.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Nakashima objected to the wood’s features; he displayed them in his furniture.

D.why_wrong: The sentence describes Nakashima’s attitude toward the wood, and a resemblance between furniture and the wood’s character makes little sense; the text points to how he treated the wood.

items.passage: Most bees obtain protein from pollen, but vulture bees, three closely related species of stingless bees in South America, feed on decomposing meat instead. Because the workers’ guts are highly acidic, the bees can safely ______ the meat, breaking it down into a substance that takes the place of pollen in the colony’s diet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To digest food is to break it down in the body so it can be used. The text says the bees’ highly acidic guts let them break the meat down into a substance that replaces pollen, so their guts allow them to digest it.

A.why_wrong: The bees feed on meat rather than avoiding it; their acidic guts are what make eating it possible.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the bees keep the meat from spoiling for later use; the text describes the meat being broken down in their guts.

D.why_wrong: An acidic gut has nothing to do with smelling; the text links the bees’ guts to breaking the meat down.

items.passage: Textile designer Dorothy Liebes was known for weaving ______ materials into her fabrics, such as feathers, ticker tape, strips of leather, and bamboo, alongside more familiar yarns. Architects including Frank Lloyd Wright commissioned her textiles, which appeared in residences, hotels, and theaters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Unconventional means unusual or not traditional. Feathers, ticker tape, leather strips, and bamboo are not what weavers normally use, and the text contrasts them with “more familiar yarns,” so Liebes wove unconventional materials into her fabrics.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about where the materials came from; the examples are unusual rather than foreign.

C.why_wrong: Feathers, ticker tape, leather, and bamboo are very different from one another, so they are not identical.

D.why_wrong: The examples include ticker tape and bamboo, which are not costly; what they share is that they are unusual in weaving.

items.passage: Animals of the intertidal zone, the stretch of shoreline exposed at low tide, are adapted to intense heat and drying out, but many could not ______ the heat wave that struck the Pacific Northwest in the summer of 2021. Temperatures on some shores reached 50°C (122°F), and more than a billion clams, barnacles, oysters, and other animals perished.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To withstand something is to survive it without being destroyed. Even though shore animals are adapted to heat, temperatures reached 50°C and more than a billion of them died, so many could not withstand the heat wave.

A.why_wrong: Animals do not measure temperatures; the text is about whether they survived the heat.

B.why_wrong: The animals did not produce the heat wave; they were its victims.

C.why_wrong: Whether the animals could see the heat wave coming is never discussed; the second sentence reports that huge numbers of them died.

sources.what: Wikipedia, 2021 Western North America heat wave: intertidal zone temperatures on the Pacific shore reached up to 50 °C (122 °F); more than a billion seashore animals such as clams, barnacles and oysters died

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine ecology). Key letter D. Negated frame (could not), with the evidence in the next sentence. Corrected ranks: measure 2,003; cause 715; anticipate 10,355; withstand 12,924.

items.passage: Among the Agta, hunter-gatherers who live in the Philippines, storytelling is not merely ______. Anthropologist Daniel Smith and colleagues found that camps with skilled storytellers were more cooperative, and that the storytellers themselves were preferred as social partners and tended to have larger families than other Agta did.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Recreational means done for enjoyment. The study links storytelling to cooperation in camps and to the storytellers’ standing and family size, so among the Agta stories do more than entertain.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests storytelling takes much time or resources; the text reports its benefits.

C.why_wrong: The study is about storytellers’ effects on cooperation and their social standing, not about whether stories are factually correct.

D.why_wrong: Storytelling among the Agta happens in camps and makes storytellers sought-after social partners, so it is a shared, social activity, not a solitary one.

sources.what: Smith et al. (2017), Cooperation and the evolution of hunter-gatherer storytelling, Nature Communications 8:1853 (PMC): among the Agta of the Philippines, good storytellers are associated with increased cooperation, are preferred social partners and have greater reproductive success
